The team agreed that scheduling logic should be centralized within the experiment entity instead of feature flags. They preferred a 'soft stop' approach, allowing experiments to pause for review rather than rollback. Additionally, it was important to simplify experiment statuses and integrate scheduling with decision frameworks to enhance clarity. The focus on these improvements aims to enhance user experience and operational efficiency.
calls.keywords: experiment scheduling, feature flags, decision framework, soft stop, UI design, scheduling logic

calls.summary: The team discussed improving the experiment scheduling process by clearly separating the scheduling intent from the actual launch readiness. Luke Sonnet and Kari Kay emphasized the need to have distinct steps for setting a start date and formally staging experiments to ensure all criteria are met before launch. They proposed a split-button UI to help users choose between starting immediately or scheduling for later while ensuring that scheduling metadata exists independently of launch confirmation. Additionally, they addressed the need for clear communication and notifications regarding experiment states, especially in cases where scheduled dates may pass without proper staging. The objective is to reduce confusion and prevent unintended launches due to incomplete prelaunch checklist or feature flags.
calls.keywords: experiment scheduling, staging, prelaunch checklist, user experience, metadata, approval flow

calls.title: luke@growthbook.io - Mon, 01 Jun 2026 12:20:19 PDT - Untitled
calls.summary: The discussion revolved around implementing a flexible ramp-up strategy for experiments, characterized by two modes: a safe rollout focusing on reversible changes and a decision-driven mode for comprehensive testing. Key elements included conditions for ramp-up based on manual input, sample sizes, and integrated guardrails to ensure safe scaling. Participants highlighted the importance of a hard end date combined with manual intervention options, allowing users to set alerts for final actions. Cleanup processes were also addressed, which will be distinct from ramp-up logic, providing users the flexibility to manage post-experiment decisions. A user-friendly interface design was emphasized to streamline scheduling and quelling actions effectively, as well as the immediate capacity for development, ensuring alignment through documentation and planning.
calls.keywords: Experiment States, Ramp-up Conditions, Guardrail Signals, Automated Rollbacks, Experiment End Date, User-Queued Decisions

calls.title: luke@growthbook.io - Tue, 30 Jun 2026 12:03:01 PDT - Untitled
calls.summary: The team focused on differentiating ramp ups and safe rollouts, where ramp ups help manage gradual traffic increases during experiments to limit potential failures, while safe rollouts ensure features are shipped with error monitoring. Luke Sonnet emphasized the need for guardrails during traffic increases, and both Luke Sonnet and Luke Smith discussed logistical constraints that support staged exposure. The importance of scoping ramp ups strictly for experiments was highlighted, avoiding complexities seen in other companies' rollout strategies. The Experiment Decision Framework (EDF) was positioned as the final decision-maker for shipping or rolling back experiments while ramp ups handle mid-experiment checks. The conversation also emphasized simplifying automation and user experiences, advocating for a clear design with a focus on user needs and minimal configurations.
calls.keywords: ramp ups, safe rollouts, guardrail monitoring, experiment decision framework, automation, experiment traffic scheduling

calls.summary: The team discussed the experiment automation framework, agreeing to focus on end-date automation for shipping while postponing ramp-ups and rollbacks for future iterations. The core automation will allow for several options, including manual and auto-shipping based on a clear winner. Next steps involve documentation and prioritizing MVP development, deferring more complex features for later.

calls.title: luke@growthbook.io - Wed, 08 Jul 2026 12:17:25 PDT - Untitled
calls.summary: The team discussed strategies for managing underperforming experiment variations by introducing two main actions: skipping, to keep current data and ongoing experiments while altering traffic visualization, and deleting, to remove variations entirely and initiate a new experiment phase for clearer data. The user interface challenges were highlighted, emphasizing the need to visually differentiate between skipped and deleted variations, with proposals for improved traffic allocation diagrams and subtle visual cues rather than overt badges. The conversation also addressed the technical complexities of linking feature flags to experiment phases, leading to inaccurate historical data portrayal, and proposed backend changes for better tracking. There was a sense of urgency to implement these changes, driven by customer demands, particularly from enterprise clients.
calls.keywords: Variation Deletion, Experiment Skipping, Traffic Allocation, Experiment Phases, UI Redesign, Decision Framework

calls.title: luke@growthbook.io - Thu, 30 Jul 2026 13:48:01 PDT - Untitled
calls.summary: The team discussed strategies to enhance feature flag integration, agreeing on the creation of separate API endpoints for creating and linking feature flags. This decision aims to clarify feature flag management, improve error handling, and align with existing REST patterns. They emphasized the flexibility of linking flags during experiment creation or later, which allows organizations to adapt their workflows. The team also recognized the importance of integrating approval workflows within the experiment flow to maintain consistency. Additionally, they addressed the need for user research on naming conventions and config handling, alongside plans for iterative development and close collaboration between teams to refine these processes.
calls.keywords: feature flag management, experiments, contextual bandit, API endpoint design, approval workflow, user experience research
